claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is a single-phase BCC alloy.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has a density greater than 12 g/cm³.
The baseline alloy has less than 5% room-temperature plastic strain and fails by brittle fracture.
Adding 2-4 at.% Si or B will precipitate an Hf-containing intermetallic phase such as Hf2Si or HfB2.
The proposed Hf2Si or HfB2 secondary phase will be ductile or sufficiently tough to impede cracking.
Heat treatment at approximately 1000-1200°C for 24 hours will promote nucleation and growth of the secondary phase.
The secondary phase will form a continuous or semi-continuous reticulated network within the BCC matrix.
A single-phase BCC RHEA is intrinsically brittle at room temperature because it has limited slip systems.
A reticulated intermetallic network will force cracks onto tortuous, deflected paths rather than allowing straight propagation through the BCC matrix.
The toughness and topology of the intermetallic network will arrest cracks and improve room-temperature ductility.
Solid-solution hardening would increase yield strength without improving ductility.
The intervention will increase compressive yield strength by 15-20% through precipitation strengthening.
The intervention will increase room-temperature plastic strain to failure from less than 5% to greater than 10%.
Adding Si or B will increase alloy density by less than 0.5 g/cm³.
The strength-ductility synergy will improve significantly relative to the baseline despite the predicted density increase.
If the secondary phase forms as isolated particles rather than a network, the ductility improvement may be negligible or negative because of particle cracking.
An increase in strength accompanied by decreased ductility would indicate solid-solution hardening or particle cracking rather than network-mediated crack deflection.
